title: Epistemology
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Study the theory of knowledge: the analysis of knowledge and the Gettier problem, theories of justification (foundationalism, coherentism, reliabilism, internalism and externalism), skepticism and its replies, a priori knowledge, perception, induction, testimony and social epistemology, and formal epistemology with credences and Bayes's theorem.

weeks.1: The analysis of knowledge: justified true belief
weeks.5: Skepticism: dreams, demons and brains in vats
weeks.6: Replies to skepticism: Moore, contextualism and closure
weeks.7: A priori knowledge and rational intuition
weeks.9: Induction and inference to the best explanation
weeks.11: Formal epistemology: credences, probability and Bayes's theorem
weeks.12: Peer disagreement and the ethics of belief

blocks.deliverable: Apply three theories of justification to the same case.
Reconstruct the closure argument for skepticism.
Week 7 midterm; evaluate one reply to skepticism.
Defend a view of when to trust testimony.
Update credences with Bayes's theorem in four cases.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Epistemology paper: write a 2,500-word paper on one problem (Gettier cases, skepticism, the a priori or peer disagreement) that reconstructs the main argument, compares two responses, and defends one, with at least one case or worked example of your own.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
